title: A New Bill Wants to Kill the H-1B Path to a Green Card. Indian Tech Workers Have the Most to Lose.
excerpt: Congressman Chip Roy's American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act would end dual intent, scrap OPT, and cut visa duration to two years — just as EB-2 India visas hit their annual ceiling
body:
Republican Congressman Chip Roy introduced the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act in the House of Representatives on June 4, upending a decades-old assumption that has shaped the career plans of hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals: that an H-1B visa is the first step toward permanent residency in America.

The bill proposes to sever the link between the H-1B programme and the green card entirely. Under current rules, H-1B holders operate under what is known as "dual intent" — they can work temporarily while simultaneously applying for permanent residency. Roy's legislation would eliminate that provision, requiring visa applicants to demonstrate that they maintain a residence abroad and have no intention of abandoning it.

The proposal does not stop there. It would scrap the Optional Practical Training programme, which allows international students to work in the United States for up to three years after graduation. It would shorten the maximum H-1B visa duration from six years to two. And it would replace the current lottery system with a salary-based selection model, where applicants offered the highest wages get priority.

https://x.com/ChipRoyTX/status/2062683867991900226

"For its nearly forty-year history, the H-1B visa has been abused, allowing employers to routinely sideline American STEM workers in favour of cheap foreign labour, while masking layoffs and wage suppression as 'shortages,'" Roy said in a statement. "It's time to end this lottery-based pipeline and replace it with a system that prioritises merit, enforces real wage standards, and puts American white-collar workers first."

The bill also includes a provision barring companies that have recently conducted mass layoffs from sponsoring H-1B workers — a direct shot at a practice that has drawn bipartisan criticism. The legislation is backed by the Federation for American Immigration Reform, the Immigration Accountability Project, and US Tech Workers. Co-sponsor Eli Crane, a Republican from Arizona, has separately proposed a three-year moratorium on all H-1B issuances.

## A System Already Under Siege

The bill arrives into an immigration landscape that has already shifted dramatically under the Trump administration. In September 2025, the president signed a proclamation imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions — a measure that effectively priced out the staffing firms and mid-tier contractors that had been the largest sponsors of Indian workers. The Department of Labor launched "Project Firewall" to target employer abuse. The Department of Housing and Urban Development barred non-permanent residents from accessing FHA-insured mortgages.

Then came the May 21 policy memo from USCIS, which instructed officers to treat adjustment of status — the process of applying for a green card from within the United States — as "extraordinary" discretionary relief rather than a routine procedure. The memo effectively made consular processing, which requires leaving the country, the default path to permanent residency.

And on the same day, the State Department confirmed that all EB-2 immigrant visas for India for fiscal year 2026 had been exhausted. No more employment-based second-preference green cards can be issued to Indian nationals until October 1 — the start of the next fiscal year. EB-2 and EB-3 priority dates for India remain stuck at January 15, 2015, meaning applicants who filed over a decade ago are still waiting.

## The Dallas Preview

The real-world consequences are already visible. In the suburbs north of Dallas — once ground zero for H-1B-driven housing demand — home prices in Collin County fell nearly 9 percent year over year as of February. The federal government granted nearly 32,000 new H-1B approvals in the Dallas area during the Biden administration, more than Silicon Valley, Seattle, or San Francisco. Indian-born residents in Frisco alone grew from 6 percent of the population in the early 2010s to nearly 20 percent by the mid-2020s.

That boom is reversing. One North Texas builder reported that South Asian buyers, who once accounted for 70 percent of his sales, now represent less than 30 percent. Immigration attorney Sharadha Kodem, who practises out of Frisco, said the anxiety among her clients is unlike anything she has seen. Those who are laid off have just 60 days to find a new employer sponsor before their visa status lapses. Some are weighing a return to India but cannot sell their homes fast enough.

"Who is there to replace them?" asked housing analyst Alex Barron.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

The bill's prospects in Congress are uncertain — immigration overhauls routinely stall, and the tech industry retains significant lobbying power. But even as a proposal, the legislation signals a hardening consensus in parts of Washington that the H-1B programme needs fundamental restructuring, not just administrative tweaks.

For the estimated 600,000 Indians currently on H-1B visas, the cumulative effect of the $100,000 fee, the AOS memo, the EB-2 exhaustion, and now Roy's bill is unmistakable: the path from temporary worker to permanent resident, already the longest in the immigration system, is narrowing from every direction at once. The question is no longer whether the system will change, but how much of the old bargain — come on a work visa, build a career, stay for good — will survive.
